findings.short_summary: Export name is unsanitized into the file path
findings.summary: The caller-supplied `name` is validated only for type and length (1–64 chars) at src/server.js:103, then joined into the filesystem path with no sanitization, so `../` sequences let an authenticated account owner write a CSV anywhere reachable by relative traversal from `exportDir` — the PR deleted the doc comment that had promised this could not happen.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /accounts/:id/export as the account's own owner with body { name: "../../../evil-marker" } passes both the type/length check and getOwnAccount's ownership check; path.join(dir, name + '.csv') then resolves outside the configured exports directory. Reproduced live against the real server: the CSV landed three directories above exportDir, outside the ledger's temp directory entirely, while the response reported only { exported: 0, file: 'evil-marker.csv' } — path.basename() in the response hides the true write location. The PR's own added test at test/server.test.js:74-77 covers only a benign name and an over-length name, so it cannot catch this.

findings.short_summary: Failed sign-in logs the raw bearer token
findings.summary: requireUser now logs `ctx.req.headers.authorization` verbatim on every failed authentication, writing the full raw bearer token — the only credential in this system — to server logs, directly contradicting this same file's doc comment that "the token is the only credential; it is never logged."
findings.failure_scenario: Any request whose Authorization header is present but matches no stored user (a guessed token, or a legitimate user's expired, rotated, or mistyped one) reaches the new console.warn at src/auth.js:25 and prints the full `Bearer <token>` string before the 401 is thrown. Verified by running the real server: a request with Authorization `Bearer super-secret-real-token-abc123` logged `sign-in failed GET /accounts with Bearer super-secret-real-token-abc123`, while a request with no header logged the safe '(no token)' placeholder. grep over src/ confirms no redaction layer exists anywhere.

findings.short_summary: Named exports silently clobber other owners' files
findings.summary: A caller-supplied export `name` is written with no existence check and no exclusive-create flag into a single flat directory shared by every account and every owner, so one owner's named export silently overwrites an unrelated owner's export file.
findings.failure_scenario: Two different owners each export one of their own accounts using the same name (a predictable choice like 'monthly-report'). The second write — plain writeFile with the default truncating 'w' flag, no existence check — silently destroys the first owner's file under the shared exportDir. Both requests return an identical-shaped 200 with no indication that anything was overwritten. Before this PR the filename was the account id, so collisions across owners were impossible.

content.text:
**Status: complete.** PR #7 at `036830a`, 3 confirmed findings, none pre-existing, nothing refuted, nothing left unverified. Result JSON written to `calibration/results/0.4.0/pr-7.json`.

All three root causes went to a full three-lens skeptic panel, and all three survived 3-of-3 — each verified by actually running the code, not just reading it. All three were reported with `corrected: true`: the skeptics sharpened the severity or wording the finders first gave them, which is why the summaries above are the corrected ones rather than the originals.

**Budget** — used 20 of 20 agents: 1 scout, 7 finders, 1 triage, 1 same-site check, 9 skeptics (three 3-lens panels), 1 critic. No ceiling was passed, so the script computed 20 as the smallest with room for every fixed angle plus two of the scout's. No retries, no agent deaths. The same-site check merged 0 groups: the two `src/export.js:18` findings are genuinely separate defects (traversal vs. collision), not one defect counted twice. The project's baseline check ran clean on this commit (`npm run check && npm test`, 22/22), so none of this is noise from a pre-broken tree.

**Angles** — 7 run: the 6 generic ones that applied, plus `secrets-in-logs (stated invariant violated)`, which the scout added after noticing the new log line contradicts `auth.js`'s own doc comment. That angle independently found the token-logging bug. The scout dropped two with reasons: `migrations-and-rollout` (no store-format change) and `authz-and-attribution` (no ownership logic changed — the export route still goes through the same `requireUser` + `getOwnAccount`). Nothing was cut by the ceiling.

**Two gaps the critic flagged** — neither was tested by a skeptic, so treat them as leads for a person, not findings:

1. `src/auth.js:24` adds an unthrottled synchronous log write on every failed-auth request. The README's own "Known limitations" says there is no rate limiting, so a documented, accepted gap now also costs a log write per attempt — log volume as a resource. The run angles all examined *what* is logged, not that logging is now attacker-triggerable at any rate.
2. `exportTransfers` has never called `record()`, unlike every other mutation in the codebase, and this PR — the change that makes the operation more dangerous by letting the caller choose the destination — still doesn't add one. There is no durable trail of who wrote which file under which name. Invisible to a line-level read because the diff doesn't touch `src/audit.js`.

The `authz-and-attribution` drop is worth a second look in light of gap 2: the reasoning was sound on its own terms (ownership logic genuinely didn't change) but it's what kept any agent from asking whether the newly-parameterised write is attributable afterwards.

Not posting, per `--no-post`. This run's 20 worktrees and branches are removed; your checkout is untouched — `main` at `7fc1c3c`, clean, one worktree as before.
